reasoning:
Executably, these two submissions are IDENTICAL. Both replace exactly one instruction at the same site in movegen.inc (line ~1180): `call moverInCheck` -> `call inCheckSide`, leaving the preceding `ld a,(sideToMove)`, the following `or a` / `jr z,utStale`, and everything else untouched. Every difference between them is comment text. I therefore score correctness_risk the same for both and discriminate only where the submissions genuinely differ (minimality, clarity).

CORRECTNESS (4 / 4). The change lands precisely on the reported fault. The bug report says the no-legal-moves detection is already right (perft passes, legal-move count is genuinely zero) and only the mate-vs-stalemate classification is wrong; the site being patched is exactly the branch that turns "no moves" into utStale vs mate. The pre-existing `ld a,(sideToMove)` immediately above the call is strong internal evidence for the diagnosis: it is dead code under `moverInCheck` (which, per Y's note, ignores A and asks about the side that just moved — never in check after a legal move, so the branch always fell to utStale, matching "every checkmate ends as a draw"), and becomes load-bearing under `inCheckSide`. The four control cases in the report all stay correct under the new code: a genuine stalemate returns not-in-check so `jr z,utStale` still fires; a check with legal replies never reaches this code because `jr nz,utHas` is taken first; and nothing on the search/eval/incremental-state path is touched, so the passing self-test and the golden render cannot regress. I withhold the fifth point (from both equally) for one thing neither diff can demonstrate: `inCheckSide`'s calling and clobber contract is not shown, so a reviewer restricted to the diff must take on faith that it consumes the side in A and returns its answer in A with the flags the following `or a` expects. Y asserts that contract and cites `utPlay` as precedent; X asserts nothing about it. That is a difference in evidence, not in behaviour, so it moves clarity rather than correctness.

MINIMALITY (X 5, Y 4). X is the irreducible fix: one token changed, one trailing comment, zero added lines. Y's functional footprint is the same single token, so its extra scope is entirely explanatory — five added comment lines, warranted in principle (this is a foot-gun: two similarly named helpers with opposite subject conventions, and the trap silently produced a wrong game result rather than a crash), but heavy relative to a one-token change, and the continuation lines sit at one space of indentation instead of aligning with the surrounding code column, which breaks the file's layout. That is a one-point deduction for verbosity and formatting, not for length as such; I did not credit or penalise either submission merely for diff size.

CLARITY (X 3, Y 5). X's "the STUCK side: in check -> mate, else stale" correctly states the intended rule, but a reviewer still has to go read both helpers to learn why the old call was wrong and why the swap cannot break genuine stalemates. Y states the defect mechanism explicitly (moverInCheck ignores A, reloads sideToMove and flips it, so it interrogates the side that just moved, which is never in check after a legal move, hence every mate was filed as stalemate), which both explains the observed symptom and makes the fix self-evidently safe for the stalemate control; the "same question as utPlay below" cross-reference is the single most useful line in either diff, because it establishes the convention the fix relies on.

MERGE: Y. The code merged is byte-for-byte what X would merge, and Y ships the root-cause note next to a helper pair that has now demonstrably misled someone once. The verbosity/indentation cost is cosmetic and cheaper than the next reader repeating the mistake; I would tidy the comment's indentation on the way in.

Blinding note: the style gap (terse trailing comment vs. a written-up root-cause block) is the kind of thing that invites a theory about differing authoring processes. I noticed the pull and deliberately did not act on it — the axis scores above rest only on the source text, and because the executable change is identical I refused to let the commentary shift correctness_risk.
